edition.note: Publisher's page (Grand Central Publishing, Hachette Book Group): hardcover ISBN 9781455509126, 304 pages, on sale Sep 18, 2012; no later edition statement. The Google Books record for the same ISBN gives Grand Central Publishing, 2012-09-18. The publisher's description names the four rules the Lessons follow: "#1: Don't follow your passion", "#2: Be so good they can't ignore you", "#3: Turn down a promotion", "#4: Think small, act big". The UK paperback and audiobook (Hachette UK, 2016, https://www.hachette.co.uk/titles/cal-newport/so-good-they-cant-ignore-you/9781405537384/) appear to be reissues; no revised edition was found, so no Lesson is known to rest on later-edition material.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Rule 1, Don't Follow Your Passion, the book's opening argument. It matters because moving to the Netherlands is a career bet, and the wrong theory of work makes you chase a feeling instead of value.
rows.note: Publisher's description lists "#1: Don't follow your passion" as the first of the four rules. The move to the Netherlands is the player profile, not a claim from the book. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: In his 2005 Stanford speech, Steve Jobs told graduates to find what they love and not settle. Newport points out that young Jobs had no clear passion: he dabbled in Western history, dance and Eastern mysticism.
rows.note: Confirmed: the author's own post says "I opened my last book with Steve Jobs's 2005 commencement address at Stanford University"; a transcript of the 12 June 2005 address (https://jamesclear.com/great-speeches/2005-stanford-commencement-address-by-steve-jobs) has "You've got to find what you love" and "keep looking. Don't settle." Not confirmed to the brief's standard: the list "Western history, dance and Eastern mysticism". Only one summary site that was opened repeats it (https://www.shortform.com/blog/why-skills-trump-passion/: "he studied dance, Western history, and a little bit of Eastern mysticism"); no official excerpt or preview showing the passage could be opened (Google Books has no preview; the Fast Company excerpt and Stanford pages returned 403). The second sentence now says only that Newport argues Jobs did not follow the advice himself and Apple was not born from a pre-existing passion, supported by Derek Sivers's notes quoting the book (https://sive.rs/book/SoGood: "Apple Computer was decidedly not born out of passion") and the Hachette UK description. English and Farsi changed together; no Check depends on this Card.

rows.claim: Robert Vallerand surveyed Canadian students: 84 percent had a passion, mostly hobbies like dance, hockey and reading. Fewer than 4 percent of the passions related to work or education.
rows.note: Globe and Mail excerpt from the book: questionnaire given to "539 Canadian university students"; "84 per cent of the students surveyed were identified as having a passion"; top five passions "dance, hockey ... skiing, reading, and swimming"; "less than 4 per cent of the total identified passions had any relation to work or education". Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Applied: "Do I love this?" is the wrong first test for a new Dutch role. Ask instead whether it lets you build skills that are rare and valuable.
rows.note: "Do I love this?" is the applied Card's own question about a Dutch role, not presented as the author's words. The idea applied is the book's: reader's notes quoting the book have "Think of these rare and valuable skills you can offer as your career capital" (secondary; https://sive.rs/book/SoGood independently has "you need rare and valuable skills to offer in return"). Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Rule 1 in one line: don't follow passion, let it follow you into good work. Skill, autonomy and connection come first, and the love for the work grows from them.
rows.note: Rule 1 as named by the publisher: "#1: Don't follow your passion". The Card's one-line summary carries no quotation marks and is not presented as the author's wording. The three needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) are listed in the calvinrosser.com notes, and the Globe and Mail excerpt confirms the book's Self-Determination Theory passage ("three basic psychological needs"). Card unchanged.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Rule 2, Be So Good They Can't Ignore You: the craftsman mindset, career capital and deliberate practice. It matters because your CTO skills are the capital you trade for equity and a paid product.
rows.note: Publisher's description: "#2: Be so good they can't ignore you". Craftsman mindset, career capital and deliberate practice appear as the rule's terms in notes quoting the book (https://calvinrosser.com/notes/so-good-they-cant-ignore-you, secondary). CTO skills, equity and a paid product are the player profile, not book claims. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Rules 3 and 4: the control traps, mission, little bets and the law of remarkability. It matters because when to quit for your own AI product is exactly the timing question the book answers.
rows.note: Publisher's description: "#3: Turn down a promotion", "#4: Think small, act big". Control traps, little bets and the law of remarkability are confirmed as the book's terms by https://calvinrosser.com/notes/so-good-they-cant-ignore-you and https://sive.rs/book/SoGood ("Little bets ... bite-sized"; "For a mission-driven project to succeed, it should be remarkable in two different ways"). The AI product is the player profile. Card unchanged.

rows.claim: Applied: your small AI product is a little bet, and the first €100 of ownership income is its viability test. Keep the job until people pay, and launch where engineers already talk.
rows.note: The first EUR 100 of ownership income is the player's roadmap goal used in an applied Card, not a figure from the book. The idea applied is the book's law of financial viability, as given in notes quoting the book: "seek evidence of whether people are willing to pay for it. If you find this evidence, continue. If not, move on." (secondary). Card unchanged.
